title: Two trumpets and parts marked by player's name
summary: As the band grew to about ten pieces, arrangers marked parts with players' names instead of first or second chair.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Why was there a need for two trumpets?

Well, as the band got bigger, you added more brass or reeds. See, after all, it started off with one trumpet, and as you get bigger, you enlarge your sections. Now, he must have been up to the point now where he had two trumpets and a trombone. I imagine that would bring him to around ten pieces, with three saxophones, and that would make him a ten-piece band, with two trumpets and a trombone.
Would Henry Allen be playing the first trumpet?

Well, he was playing... No, I would say Red was playing first trumpet. Otis would be playing the first trumpet. And some... Well, I mean, it was intermittent. Some numbers Red would be playing first trumpet. But they did away with that first trumpet part, and one-thing-or-another, and they started marking the music, the arranger would start marking the music, "Henry Allen" or "Otis Johnson," "Charlie Holmes"... He'd mark the parts by the name. You didn't know what you was playing. I mean, no first or third or second...
So it was that intimate a band that Russell would be writing for the musicians...

No. That went on with most of the bands at the time, to get away from that first part. Just because sometimes, I mean, you'd be playing the first part and you'd be playing the third part -- you'd be playing any parts. You would just be playing the parts.

Sure. I mean, that would stop a whole lot of this-that-and-the-other, if I'm the first trumpet player and I'm not a this kind of trumpet player -- it stopped all of that, and you just played the part. It's your part, it's got your name on it -- play it.
